terms.definition: The sum of all the values divided by how many values there are. It answers what each observation would receive if the total were shared out equally, it carries the same unit as the data, and multiplying it by the number of observations returns the total. Every value enters it at full weight, so a value far out in a tail pulls it toward that tail.

The middle value once the observations are placed in order, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even. It answers which value splits the group in half. Because it is determined by ranks rather than by magnitudes, changing how extreme an extreme value is does not move it.

For a sample, the exact value that occurs most often. It is informative for data recorded as a small number of fixed levels or categories. In finely measured continuous samples, exact repeats depend on measurement precision, so a modal histogram interval or a population-density mode can be more informative. A distribution can have more than one mode.

A summary whose value changes little when a small number of extreme observations change. The median and the quartiles are resistant; the mean, the range, and the standard deviation are not. Resistance is a property to choose deliberately, because a summary that ignores a change in the extremes also fails to report one that matters.

One observation minus the mean of its data set, carrying a sign and the unit of the data. The deviations of any data set sum to zero, which is why a spread measure squares them before averaging rather than averaging them directly.

In this lesson, a single number that measures spread: the largest value in a data set minus the smallest, carrying the same unit as the data. It uses only the two most extreme observations, so one unusual or mistyped value can change it dramatically.

alignment.note: PREM-QNT-007 defines range as the set of outputs a function produces over its declared domain, which is a collection of values. The statistical sense used here is a different technical meaning of the same word: one number, the maximum minus the minimum of an observed data set, with the unit of the data. The two senses are bridged in the scene where the term is introduced so a learner meeting both is not left to reconcile them alone.

terms.definition: One of the three values that cut an ordered data set into four parts of equal size. The lower quartile Q1 sits at the 25th percentile, the second quartile is the median, and the upper quartile Q3 sits at the 75th percentile. Software packages use slightly different interpolation rules, so reported quartiles can differ a little on the same small sample.

The upper quartile minus the lower quartile, that is the width of the middle half of an ordered data set, in the unit of the data. It describes variability near the centre and is usually less sensitive to outliers than the range.

The minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, and maximum of a data set, reported in that order. Together they describe where the middle half sits and how far each side reaches, which a single centre value cannot do. Those distances can warn that the sides differ, but they do not identify distribution shape without a plot or the raw values.

The sum of the squared deviations from the mean divided by one less than the number of observations, for a sample. Squaring removes the signs so the deviations do not cancel, at the cost of leaving the result in squared units, such as mg squared per dL squared for glucose data.

The square root of the variance, which returns the spread to the unit of the original data. Read it as roughly the distance a typical observation sits from the mean, in either direction. Because it shares the data's unit, it can be set beside a mean, a group difference, or a measurement precision and compared directly, and dividing a difference by it produces a quantity with no unit at all.

A distribution that looks the same to the left and to the right of its centre point. If the mean exists and the median is unique, both lie at that centre. A mode lies there only with an additional unimodal, single-central-mode condition. Mean-median agreement alone does not establish symmetry and can also occur in skewed or separated data.

The lack of symmetry in a distribution. A distribution is skewed right when its right tail is long relative to its left, and skewed left when its left tail is longer. A long right tail often lifts the mean above the median and a long left tail often lowers it, but the comparison is not a universal shape test.

An observation that sits far from the bulk of the data. The label describes a position in the distribution and nothing more; an outlier may be a recording error, or it may be an accurate measurement of a person whose situation genuinely differs from the rest, and deciding which is a matter for the investigator rather than for the arithmetic.
